threads_text: Anthropic secretly told Claude which side to argue on each choice, decided by a coin flip, and 50 professional analysts ended up agreeing with it 86% of the time. Only 15% gave the AI any credit for their thinking. Would you notice if an AI was steering your decisions?
caption:
Anthropic gave 50 professional analysts Claude Code and a policy question to answer.
A hidden coin flip decided which option Claude would argue for on each key choice.
The analysts matched Claude's lean 86% of the time, and only 15% credited the AI.

Would you notice if an AI was nudging your decisions?

site_article.headline: Anthropic study finds analysts followed Claude's planted preferences 86 percent of the time
site_article.dek: In a controlled test, a hidden coin flip set which option the AI argued for, and professional analysts mostly went along without crediting it.
site_article.summary: Anthropic published a study on October 27, 2026 in which 50 professional analysts using Claude Code matched the agent's secretly assigned preference on 86 percent of key analysis choices. Only 15 percent credited the AI for their reasoning, even though 77 percent repeated its arguments.
site_article.seo_title: Anthropic study: experts followed Claude's planted lean 86% of time
site_article.seo_description: In an Anthropic test, 50 analysts using Claude Code matched a coin-flip preference planted in the AI on 86% of decisions, and few credited it.
site_article.answer_summary: Yes, in Anthropic's test experts deferred heavily to the AI: analysts matched a randomly assigned Claude preference on 86 percent of choices, against about 50 percent expected by chance.
site_article.hero_alt: The Anthropic logo displayed at the Moscone Center in San Francisco during a technology conference.

paragraphs.text: Anthropic published a study on October 27, 2026 showing that professional analysts who worked with its AI agent largely adopted the agent's position on key judgment calls, even when that position had been set at random. The researchers, Amaç Herdağdelen, Hailey Joren and Alex Tamkin of Anthropic's Alignment team, said analysts matched the agent's lean 86 percent of the time, compared with roughly 50 percent expected by chance.

Anthropic recruited 61 professional analysts with experience in observational causal inference who regularly use Python or R. Eleven chose not to use the agent and were left out of the main analysis, leaving 50. Each analyst used Claude Code in VS Code, running Claude Opus 4.8, to advise a fictional farming cooperative called Greenfields on whether to expand or discontinue a voluntary, paid advisory program for its members.

The task included four analytical choices with two defensible options each: the outcome measure, the comparison method, which farms to include and how to weight them. A fifth decision was the final recommendation. For each choice, a coin flip secretly set which option the agent favored. The agent was told to hold that lean, argue for it honestly and change its mind only if the evidence required it. The analysts did not know about the planted preferences.

Across the four analytical choices, analysts matched the agent's lean 86 percent of the time, with rates between 81 and 92 percent depending on the decision. In 38 cases where analysts stated their own preference first, they switched 60 percent of the time when the agent disagreed and 6 percent of the time when it agreed, according to the study. The final recommendation moved too: 54 percent recommended expanding the program when the agent leaned that way, compared with 36 percent when it did not, a gap Unite.AI notes was not statistically significant under the primary estimator.

The influence was largely invisible to the participants. According to Anthropic, 77 percent of analysts repeated the agent's arguments, sometimes nearly word for word, but only 15 percent credited the agent. On a survey after the task, 52 percent rated the recommendation as more their own than the agent's. Experience did not predict who deferred.

The study also found that AI help reduced mistakes. Six of 11 analysts who worked without the agent made serious methodological errors, compared with 3 of 50 who used it. Anthropic cautioned that the groups chose themselves and the no-AI group was less experienced, so the comparison does not show cause and effect.

The authors said they deliberately strengthened the agents' leans, so effects in everyday use may be smaller, and that the test covered one task, one field and one model. They warned that keeping a human in the loop assumes the person's judgment is an independent check, and that this deference is hard to spot, even for the experts themselves, as Al Jazeera reported. They suggested agents that present the strongest case for each option or ask for the expert's view first.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the finding matters less for the farming task than for the many places where a human signature is treated as proof of independent review, from research reports to safety checks on AI systems. If an agent's default preferences can quietly carry through a reviewer's work, the review itself needs a design that brings out the reviewer's own view before the AI weighs in.

Watch whether Anthropic and other AI developers change how coding and research agents present choices, for example by laying out both options or asking for the user's view first, as the study suggests.
